title: Book of the Dead, Spell 128: Adorations to Osiris (papyrus of Iuefankh)
source: Papyrus of Iuefankh, Turin, Museo Egizio Cat. 1791 (Museo Egizio photographs, CC0) + TLA transliteration (ed. B. Backes, CC BY-SA 4.0) + English of Samuel Birch (1867, public domain)
description: Spell 128 of the Book of the Dead in the Turin papyrus of Iuefankh (Ptolemaic period): adorations to Osiris, with the TLA transliteration and Birch's 1867 English.
introduction:
The Book of the Dead, in Egyptian the spells for going forth by day, is a collection of funerary spells written on papyrus rolls and placed in burials from the New Kingdom to the Roman period. Each roll was made for one person, with spells taken from a large repertoire and illustrated with drawings (vignettes). This library gives one complete roll: the papyrus of Iuefankh in the Museo Egizio, Turin (Cat. 1791), written in the Ptolemaic period (332-30 BCE) and coming from Thebes. Richard Lepsius published it in 1842 and divided it into 165 chapters; his numbering is still the standard numbering of the spells, and it is used here.

Spell 128 (Birch: 'The chapter of Adorations to Osiris.') is on Lepsius's plates LI-LII and on photographs 20, 21 of the 31 Museo Egizio photographs of the roll.

The Egyptian is the transliteration of the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae (edition by Burkhard Backes), with the column number of the spell before each column; the numbers are those of Lepsius's plates. On the papyrus the text runs in vertical columns of cursive hieroglyphs from right to left along the roll; titles and some words are written in red. Signs restored by the editor are in square brackets, signs the scribe left out in angle brackets, superfluous signs in braces and damaged signs in half brackets. The English is the translation by Samuel Birch, published in 1867 and made from Lepsius's copy of this papyrus, so the English and the Egyptian come from the same manuscript. It was the first complete English translation of the Book of the Dead; many passages are now understood differently. Birch's own square brackets give his alternatives and explanations. The photographs are by the Museo Egizio; each shows a stretch of the roll, and the note of each section says where the spell stands on it.
translator_notes: Birch's English was taken from three scans of Bunsen's Egypt's Place in Universal History, vol. V (1867), on the Internet Archive. The three OCR texts were aligned word by word and each word was settled by their agreement; running heads, page numbers, footnote markers and footnotes were removed. Some OCR errors may remain, chiefly in proper names.
Birch uses the terms and name forms of his time: Hades, Aahlu (Elysium), Tum for Atum, Seb for Geb, Anup for Anubis, Phoenix or Bennu for the heron.
Labels such as 'title line' or 'gate 1' before a line of the Egyptian translate the position labels of the TLA.
The TLA has no hieroglyphic encoding for these texts, so only the transliteration is shown.

translation.text:
CXXVIII. The chapter of Adorations to Osiris.

[Vignette — Deceased adoring Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Nephthys]

Hail, oh Osiris! revealer of good, justified, son of Nu, the eldest son of Seb, the great one proceeding from Nu, the King dwelling in the midst of the regions of the great winds, dwelling in the West, Lord of Abydos [East], Lord of things created, greatest of Spirits, Lord of the crown, in Suten khennu [Bubastis], Lord prevailing in the region of the great winds, Lord of the house, greatest of the Spirits in Tattu, Lord of numerous things and festivals in Tattu! Horus proclaims his father Osiris everywhere. Isis and her sister Nephthys follow. Thoth speaks by the great intelligence which is in his belly and comes out of his mouth, welcomed is Horus by the Gods. Lead on Horus, son of Isis, support thou thy father Osiris.

Oh Osiris! I have come to thee. I am Horus, I have avenged, I have lived this day off meals of food and drink, oxen and geese, and all the good things of Osiris. Mayest thou be led along! Oh Osiris! I have smitten for thee thy enemies. I have been avenged upon them. I Horus, upon that good day, on a good festival, with thy Spirits. He has been proclaimed by him on that day to thy followers [thy companions].

Hail, Osiris! thou hast come, thy genius with thee. Thou art at peace in the name of Ka and Hetp. He is (the genius) spiritualised under the name of Akhu, he is adored under the name of Kfa. He has got ready thy path under the name of Apheru. Oh Osiris! I have come to thee. I place all thy enemies under thee everywhere, thou art justified before the Associate Gods!

Oh Osiris! seize thy mace, place thy steps under thee pass the food of the Gods, pass the food of those who are in their resting-places. Give thou thy greatness to Gods, thou hast been made the Great God, thou art with them as their mummy, thou wilt prevail over the Gods, thou hast listened to Truth on that day.

Said offering to that God on the Uka festival.

Photograph 20 of 31 (Commons Book_of_the_Dead_of_Iuefankh,_papyrus_-_Museo_Egizio_Turin_C_1791_p015.jpg): the gods and the adoring man at 6-17%; its last columns are at the right-hand edge of photograph 21. Photograph 21 of 31 (Commons Book_of_the_Dead_of_Iuefankh,_papyrus_-_Museo_Egizio_Turin_C_1791_p014.jpg): its last columns at the right-hand edge (95-100%). Checked by eye: the photographs were matched to Lepsius's plates by their vignettes, red titles and framed compartments, and the overlapping edges of neighbouring photographs were compared.

Positions in the notes are measured from the left edge of the photograph.
